item.title: Selecting End-Of-Arm Tooling for Cobots
item.description:
End effectors enable cobots to handle components and perform production tasks reliably

Source: Wong/stock.adobe.com, generated with AI

The success of an industrial cobot depends on many factors. One of them is how the cobot interacts with the workpiece. For example, during computer numerical control (CNC) machine tending, a coolant-coated component can slip from the tooling as the arm accelerates away from the machine.

Reach, payload, speed, and repeatability are often the starting points when manufacturers evaluate cobots. These specifications describe the arm’s motion and load capacity. However, they do not indicate how reliably it can handle a particular component or perform a production task.

End-of-arm tooling (EOAT) provides this interaction through a device attached to the robot wrist. EOAT design affects how reliably the robot handles components and whether the operation meets cycle time requirements. It also affects the safety of the workers sharing the workspace.

In the last part of our cobot blog series, we detailed how machine vision enhances motion capabilities. This final blog in the series explores the primary cobot tooling mechanisms, the key criteria for selecting EOAT based on the workpiece, and the critical integration requirements for safe, reliable cobot operation.

Mechanism Selection: Matching Tooling to the Application

EOAT can be divided into two groups: handling tools that move workpieces and process tools that perform industrial manufacturing operations.

Handling tools typically involve various grippers and gripper jaws. Mechanical grippers clamp components using moving jaws. Parallel jaws move along straight paths to grasp opposing faces. Angular jaws allow the fingers to clear fixtures during loading.

When parts have different shapes or arrive out of position, fixed fingers can become restrictive. Adaptive grippers use linkages or compliant joints that conform to the object to reduce the need for a separate finger design. Soft grippers use flexible materials to spread contact pressure, making them suitable for delicate products.

Other tools hold parts without closing fingers around them. Vacuum grippers use a pressure difference at the suction point to lift the object. They can also handle packaged goods if the surface provides sufficient sealing. Magnetic grippers attract ferromagnetic materials and can transfer compatible steel blanks into a machine.

Process EOAT has a very different purpose. Screwdrivers tighten fasteners to a controlled torque, while welding torches join metal parts. Dispensing tools lay adhesive or sealant along a defined path. Sanding and polishing tools control abrasive contact with a surface. These process tools allow the cobot to complete an operation rather than simply transport the workpiece.

Design Variables: Evaluating the Workpiece and Process for EOAT Selection

Engineers can start the tool selection process by understanding the workpiece requirements, such as its dimensions, load, and geometry. These factors determine where the tool can make contact. While material and surface condition affect grip reliability, stiffness and fragility limit the pressure it can tolerate.

Consider a machined steel part. Mechanical fingers can grasp a shoulder, a magnetic gripper can lift a compatible steel component, and a vacuum gripper can grip a sufficiently smooth, nonporous face. But the choice will depend on the available surface area, since the holding force needs to counter acceleration and orientation changes.

Engineers should also allow for part variation, acceptable surface marks, and possible deformation. They need to establish what happens if power or air fails. Grip and release times must fit the production cycle.

In addition, the selected tool will affect robot loading. Payload consists of the tool, hoses, cables, fittings, and the workpiece. Additional weight further away from the cobot wrist results in more torque and angular inertia. Thus, an assembly that is below the nominal load capacity will still be over the permissible wrist loads.

Another aspect to understand is the operating environment. Dust or water may harm the seals and mechanisms. Electronics processing requires electrostatic discharge (ESD) protection while hazardous environments need certified tools.

Throughout all these considerations, the best tool is the one that performs reliably under real-world industrial production conditions.

System Architecture: Integrating the Tool with the Complete Cobot System

Mounting the tool to the wrist is the first step towards integration. The flange and adapter need to maintain alignment without excessive flexing. Cables and hoses also need clearance throughout the arm’s motion to prevent snagging or fatigue.

After the mounting process, the controller has to calibrate the Tool Center Point (TCP). This gives a description of the location and orientation of the working point with respect to the wrist. An incorrect calibration can result in mistakenly positioning a screwdriver bit off the fastener, even with correct movement of the arm.

Operating the tool requires discrete electrical input/output (I/O), industrial communication protocols, or pneumatic valves. Feedback gives confirmation on the presence of the parts, sufficient gripping force, or vacuum. But for process tooling, verification of completion gives assurance that the fastening has been done properly.

For high-mix production, automatic tool changers let one cobot switch from handling a part to performing an operation. This reduces manual changeovers, but the changer also requires docking stations, utility connections, and tool-specific calibration.

The safety measures of collaborative arms’ tooling are also very important for floor operators. Powered tools can cause severe injuries, as in the case of a heated surface causing burns. Therefore, risk assessment should cover the arm, tool, workpiece, process, and surrounding equipment together.

Reliability also depends on the maintenance of cobots. Monitoring tool feedback and replacing worn components before failure helps maintain consistent gripping and process quality.

Conclusion

To ensure reliable operations across applications, end-of-arm tooling converts a cobot’s programmed motion into useful production work. Selecting the right tool begins with understanding the workpiece and the process it must support, followed by the conditions it will encounter in production.

Engineers need to balance reliable operation with the capacity and cycle time requirements. Utility needs and maintenance demands also influence the design, along with the safety of the complete application.

Carefully selected and integrated EOAT can extend the same cobot platform across different tasks. However, this flexibility provides value only when each operation performs consistently under actual production conditions.

item.title: New Tech Tuesdays: Compact Surge Protection for Demanding Power Systems
item.description:
New Tech Tuesdays

Join Mouser's Technical Content team for a weekly look at all things interesting, new, and noteworthy for design engineers.

Severe weather and other environmental factors regularly cause power grid faults, sometimes resulting in outages or surges. While flickering lights and blinking digital clocks are just a mild inconvenience, these grid faults can not only significantly disrupt sensitive electronics by interrupting communications, resetting embedded controllers, or overstressing power stages, but also damage electronic systems.

This week’s New Tech Tuesdays examines the causes of electrical surges, the design considerations behind compact surge protection, and how thermal disconnects and status monitoring improve protection coordination and system reliability.

When Microseconds Mean Danger

Electrical transients can originate outside the equipment from lightning-related disturbances and utility switching, or inside it when inductive loads, contactors, and motors are switched. Although these transients may last only a short time, the resulting voltage and current can exceed the normal operating envelope of power semiconductors, controllers, communications interfaces, and insulation systems.

A surge protective device (SPD) limits exposure to dangerous voltage and current levels by diverting surge current and constraining voltage for downstream circuitry. Metal-oxide varistors (MOVs) are well-suited to this task because they create a temporary current path around the protected load when the applied voltage exceeds their characteristic threshold, causing their resistance to drop sharply.

Why Compact Surge Protection Is a System Problem

In many designs, space remains one of engineering’s most constrained resources. Minimizing enclosure volume and printed circuit board (PCB) area reduces manufacturing and shipping costs, so designers often find themselves optimizing for size.

Size constraints encourage layered protection. No single component substitutes for coordination across the installation. An upstream SPD can absorb a large portion of an incoming event, while protection closer to a control panel or load can reduce the remaining stress. Short, direct connections also add a layer of protection because lead and trace inductance can add voltage during rapid current changes.

The Heat Behind the Clamp

An MOV absorbs energy each time it conducts. However, repeated surges, temporary overvoltage, or operating beyond rated conditions can change its characteristics and increase leakage current over time. That leakage produces heat, and under abnormal sustained conditions, this can lead to a thermal runaway.

A thermally protected varistor addresses this failure mode by connecting a thermal disconnect in series just next to the MOV. If the varistor overheats, the disconnect opens the current path, preventing a thermal runaway.

MOVs are connected in parallel to their loads, so a circuit can continue operating even after a thermal fuse disconnects the varistor. A remote indication contact or visual indicator notifies a controller or maintenance technician that the protection element has opened. That turns a hidden loss of protection into a service event that can be logged and corrected.

Selecting Protection Without Guesswork

Protection selection begins with the power source. The selected maximum continuous operating voltage must withstand normal line variations, and the clamping performance must remain fast enough to protect downstream equipment. AC and DC ratings are not interchangeable assumptions; designers should use the values specified for the intended operating mode.

Once the parameters for normal operation are determined, designers can then test against surges using the applicable equipment, installation, and regional standards. The standard 8/20μs pulse is used to simulate lightning strikes and switching transients with a nominal virtual front time of 8μs and a half-value time of 20μs.

Engineers also need to consider manufacturability when thermal fuses are involved in the design. Thermal fuses generally cannot undergo reflow soldering and require either manual soldering or wave soldering.

The Newest Products for Your Newest Designs®

Bringing surge suppression, thermal safety, and status monitoring together in a compact design is an approach TDK uses to address the protection demands of modern power systems. TDK MT40 Series ThermoFuse varistors combine a strap-terminated MOV with an integrated thermal disconnect in a 38.0mm × 15.2mm × 40.9mm package. The series supports maximum continuous operating AC voltages from 150V to 550V and DC voltages from 200V to 750V, with a nominal discharge-current rating of 20kA for 15 pulses and a peak surge-current capability of 50kA for one pulse, both using an 8/20μs pulse.

For fault coordination, the MT40 series varistors provide a short-circuit current rating (SCCR) of up to 200kA according to UL 1449 and are recognized as a UL 1449 Type 1CA component assembly for AC and DC applications. A galvanically isolated, normally open micro-switch supports remote status indication. The variants share a common electrode footprint, which can simplify board reuse across voltage options.

The operating temperature range is −40°C to +85°C, and the encapsulation is rated UL 94 V-0. MT40 ThermoFuse varistors offer solutions in several applications, including photovoltaic systems, industrial power supplies, outdoor lighting, telecommunications systems, and SPD assemblies.

Tuesday’s Takeaway

Compact surge protection works best when engineers account for it throughout the power architecture. MOV ratings must align with the operating voltage and expected surge environment, while connection length, grounding, fault current, temperature, and layered coordination determine how effectively the system performs.

Designs are moving toward an integrated thermal disconnect that isolates an overheated varistor, while the status contact indicates when surge protection is no longer available. For industrial and energy equipment, that combination can reduce protection-system complexity while preserving the monitoring and maintenance visibility needed for reliable operation.

item.title: MOSFET FAQs: 10 Essential Questions Answered
item.description:
Image Source: ALEKSFILM/stock.adobe.com

The sudden, unmistakable pop of a failing power device is a sound familiar to any engineer. More often than not, that acoustic failure indicates that a power semiconductor has been pushed past its limits by electrical, thermal, or transient overstress.

Although the world of power electronics is changing, silicon-based MOSFETs remain the most common type. To clear up common ambiguities in terminology, type, structure, usage, and selection, this guide focuses on silicon MOSFETs and answers 10 essential questions to help engineers with this mainstay electronic component.

What Does MOSFET Stand For?

MOSFET is an acronym for metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor. Each part of the name describes an aspect of its construction or operation:

  • Metal: The gate electrode of the MOS structure. Although modern devices do not always use a metallic gate material, the original terminology has been retained.
  • Oxide: The gate insulator layer, traditionally silicon dioxide.
  • Semiconductor: The silicon substrate forming the conductive channel.
  • Field effect: The voltage-driven control mechanism modulating conductivity via an electric field.
  • Transistor: A semiconductor device that controls current or voltage and can be used for switching or amplification.

What Is a MOSFET?

A MOSFET is a voltage-controlled semiconductor used to switch or amplify signals. Unlike bipolar junction transistors (BJTs), MOSFETs do not require continuous control current during conduction, although their gates require transient current during switching.

While structurally a four-terminal device, the body is usually tied to the source, creating three terminals (Figures 1 and 2):

  • Gate (G): The isolated control terminal that establishes the internal electric field.
  • Drain (D): One of the two main current-carrying terminals. In conventional first-quadrant operation of an N-channel MOSFET, conventional current enters the drain and leaves the source, although an enhanced channel can conduct in either direction.
  • Source (S): The reference terminal for gate-source voltage (VGS) and one of the main current-carrying terminals.

An insulating dielectric layer separates the gate from the channel, providing high input impedance by blocking DC conduction. This allows a gate voltage to efficiently control the current between source and drain.

Figure 1: The schematic symbol for an N-channel MOSFET, with the gate, drain, and source labelled. (Source: Public Domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=829685)

Figure 2: The schematic symbol for a P-channel MOSFET, with the gate, source, and drain labelled. (Source: Public Domain, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MOSFET#/media/File:IGFET_P-Ch_Enh_Labelled.svg)

How Does a MOSFET Differ from Other Transistors?

The MOSFET is a type of field-effect transistor (FET) that uses an insulated gate to control current flow between the drain and source terminals. The following are some of the key differences between MOSFETs and BJTs:

  • Control parameter: Silicon MOSFETs are voltage-controlled devices that rely on the gate-source voltage (VGS), whereas BJTs are controlled by the base current (IB).
  • Input impedance: Silicon MOSFETs have extremely high input impedance because the gate is insulated from the channel, while BJTs typically exhibit much lower input impedance.
  • Drive requirements: MOSFETs require very little steady-state gate current, simplifying the design of gate-drive circuits. BJTs require a continuous base current while conducting.
  • Switching speeds: MOSFETs generally switch faster than comparable power BJTs, making them well-suited for switching power supplies, motor drives, and other high-frequency applications.
  • Temperature coefficient: When fully enhanced in the ohmic region, silicon power MOSFETs generally exhibit a positive temperature coefficient of RDS(on), which can improve static current sharing between properly matched and thermally coupled parallel devices.

These characteristics have made MOSFETs widely used in high-frequency switching and power-conversion applications, particularly at low and moderate voltage levels. Higher switching frequencies also enable the use of smaller magnetic components, helping create more compact and efficient systems.

What Is a MOSFET Used For?

MOSFETs are widely used for power switching, load control, signal amplification, and digital logic. Most applications can be grouped into four key areas:

  • Power switching: The dominant switching device in DC-DC converters, switched-mode power supplies, inverters, and motor drives.
  • Signal amplification: Used in many audio amplifiers, Radio frequency (RF) power stages, analogue integrated circuits, and active-load configurations.
  • Logic circuits: Paired as complementary N-channel and P-channel devices to form energy-efficient Complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) logic used throughout modern digital electronics.
  • Power distribution and load switching: Used as solid-state switches in battery management systems, eFuses, power-path control, hot-swap protection, and general load switching.

Explore more MOSFET use cases from a practical motor drive perspective in the Basics of MOSFETs and IGBTs for Motor Control application analysis.

How Does a MOSFET Work?

A MOSFET is controlled by the gate-to-source voltage (VGS), which determines whether current can flow between the drain and source. In an enhancement-mode MOSFET, the device is normally off, meaning little or no current flows when VGS is zero.

When a positive voltage is applied to the gate of an N-channel MOSFET, an electric field is created across the insulating oxide layer. This field attracts electrons toward the semiconductor surface beneath the gate, eventually creating a conductive channel. Once the gate voltage exceeds the threshold voltage (VTH), current can flow through this channel from the drain to the source.

Increasing the gate voltage strengthens this channel, reducing the device’s on-resistance (RDS(on)) and allowing it to conduct more efficiently.

What Are the Main Types of MOSFETs?

MOSFETs are commonly classified by their channel type (N-channel or P-channel) and operating mode (enhancement or depletion). Combining these characteristics produces four fundamental MOSFET variants:

  • N-channel enhancement mode: The most common type used in power electronics. It is a normally OFF device that requires a positive VGS for conduction. Because electrons have higher mobility than holes in silicon, N-channel devices typically offer lower RDS (on), higher current capability, and better overall efficiency than equivalent P-channel devices.
  • P-channel enhancement mode: A normally OFF device requiring a negative VGS to conduct. These are often used in high-side switching applications because they simplify gate-drive circuitry for positive supply rails.
  • N-channel depletion mode: A normally ON device with a pre-existing channel. A current-conducting channel exists at VGS = 0V, so a negative VGS is required to deplete the channel and turn the device OFF. These devices are typically used in specialised applications, such as constant-current circuits, startup circuits, and fail-safe designs.
  • P-channel depletion mode: A normally ON device requiring a positive VGS to turn OFF. This is the least common MOSFET variant, typically found in specialised analogue and process-specific applications.

For a deeper look into selecting these specific types, see the Ultimate Guide to Silicon MOSFET Technology.

What Is the Structure of a MOSFET?

The physical construction of an N-channel enhancement-mode MOSFET is built on a P-type silicon substrate. Two heavily doped N+ regions are formed in the substrate to serve as the source and drain. Above the area between them sits a thin layer of insulating silicon dioxide (SiO₂), topped by the gate electrode (Figure 3). The oxide layer insulates the gate from the underlying silicon, which gives rise to the device’s high input impedance.

Figure 3: A cross-sectional diagram showing the internal structure of a MOSFET, highlighting the N-type and P-type materials, the oxide layer, and metal contacts. (Source: Mouser)

MOSFETs are available in three main structure types:

  • Planar: These use a channel formed near the silicon surface. In power MOSFETs, current flows through a surface channel before passing vertically through the device to the drain.
  • Trench: Vertical trenches contain the gate electrode and gate dielectric, forming channels along the trench sidewalls. This arrangement can increase cell density and reduce on-resistance, particularly in low- and medium-voltage power MOSFETs.
  • Superjunction: This structure uses alternating columns of P-type and N-type material to improve the trade-off between breakdown voltage and on-resistance, enabling lower conduction losses at higher voltages.

How Do You Test a MOSFET on a Circuit Board?

When testing a MOSFET, initial diagnostics can be performed in-circuit, but definitive testing often requires removing the device.

The following steps present a typical troubleshooting process:

  1. Power down: Disconnect power and discharge all capacitors before making resistance or diode measurements.
  2. Check for shorts: With the gate discharged and held at the source potential, use a multimeter to check for an unintended low-resistance drain-to-source path. Use diode-test mode to check for the expected intrinsic body-diode conduction in the polarity appropriate to the device. These checks can identify gross failures but do not validate all MOSFET characteristics.
  3. Verify circuit operation: If energized testing can be performed safely, use appropriately rated differential or isolated measurement equipment to inspect the gate-to-source and drain-to-source waveforms. Do not connect an earth-referenced oscilloscope probe to a switching node unless the measurement arrangement is specifically designed for it.
  4. Remove and test, if necessary: If measurements prove inconclusive, remove the MOSFET from the PCB and test it separately. This eliminates the influence of surrounding components and provides a more reliable assessment of device health.

How Do You Use a MOSFET in a Circuit?

The exact implementation depends on the application, but most MOSFET switching circuits require attention to gate drive, load protection, thermal management, and PCB layout. Common design considerations include:

  • Gate-drive voltage: Ensure the available gate-drive voltage is sufficient to fully enhance the MOSFET. The threshold voltage (VTH) indicates when conduction begins, not when the device reaches its specified low RDS(on).
  • Gate resistor selection: A series resistor placed close to the gate pin helps control gate charging and discharging currents, manage switching speed, and reduce ringing and parasitic oscillation.
  • Gate-to-source bias resistor: A resistor between the gate and source pins returns VGS to the device’s off-state value when the driver is inactive or in high-impedance mode. This is commonly called a pull-down resistor for a ground-referenced N-channel MOSFET.
  • Flyback diode placement: When switching inductive loads such as relays, solenoids, or motors, a flyback diode is placed across the load to suppress potentially damaging voltage spikes during turn-off.
  • Heat dissipation considerations: Conduction and switching losses generate heat within the MOSFET. Calculating these losses helps determine whether a heatsink or additional cooling is required.
  • Layout optimisation: Minimising the inductance of gate and power loops helps reduce voltage overshoot, ringing, electromagnetic interference (EMI), and potential device stress.

What MOSFET Should I Buy?

MOSFET selection typically involves these key application-level requirements:

  • Voltage rating: Choose a VDS rating comfortably above the highest operating and transient voltages.
  • Current and conduction losses: Use the expected load current and RDS(on) to estimate conduction losses and temperature rise.
  • Gate-drive compatibility: Ensure the available gate voltage is sufficient to fully enhance the MOSFET.
  • Switching performance: For high-frequency applications, evaluate parameters such as gate charge (Qg) and output capacitance.
  • Package and thermal management: Verify that the package and cooling arrangement can safely dissipate the expected power loss.
  • Device technology: Trench MOSFETs generally dominate lower-voltage applications, while superjunction devices are widely used at higher voltages.

For a more in-depth guide on device selection, see the Ultimate Guide to Silicon MOSFET Technology, which offers a step-by-step process for selecting a silicon MOSFET.

Knowing When to Choose MOSFET Alternatives

While silicon MOSFETs are often a great choice for many applications, some alternatives can offer significant advantages under specific operating conditions:

  • IGBTs: Often preferred in very high-power and high-voltage applications where switching frequencies are relatively low, such as wind turbines and large industrial motor drives.
  • Silicon carbide (SiC) MOSFETs: Preferred for high-efficiency, high-temperature, and high-voltage power conversion. Currently popular for electric vehicle (EV) traction systems and high-power EV chargers.
  • Gallium nitride (GaN) FETs: Ideal for ultra-high switching frequencies and high-power-density designs. Found in compact USB Type-C smartphone chargers and laptop power supplies.

For a detailed comparative breakdown for your technology selection, see Mouser’s guide on MOSFETs versus IGBTs. To source components for an active design, explore Mouser’s full inventory of MOSFETs.

item.title: MOSFET vs. IGBT: Choosing the Correct Switch for Your Power Application
item.description:
Choosing between a metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) and an insulated-gate bipolar transistor (IGBT) is one of the most important decisions in power electronics design. The selected switch influences efficiency, power density, thermal performance, system cost, and achievable switching frequency.

Why MOSFET vs. IGBT Switching Matters in Power Electronics

Power semiconductors form the backbone of modern power electronics design. MOSFETs and IGBTs are the two dominant options, each with distinct operating characteristics. Selecting the wrong switching device can result in failure to meet efficiency targets, thermal issues, or development cost overruns in inverters, motor drives, switching power supplies, and power converters. For foundational context, explore MOSFET FAQs: 10 Essential Questions Answered.

MOSFET vs. IGBT Device Characteristics

MOSFETs and IGBTs differ in several important respects:

  • MOSFET: A voltage-controlled device that can achieve switching frequencies in the megahertz range. Silicon MOSFETs are deployed in applications ranging from low-voltage systems to systems operating at up to 900V, with devices rated at 1,200V and above available.
  • IGBT: A voltage-controlled device that combines a MOSFET input structure with a bipolar transistor output. Designers select IGBTs for their robustness in higher-voltage applications (up to 6,500V) or where switching speeds of 20kHz to 50kHz are acceptable.

For device structural variants, explore Mouser’s Ultimate Guide to Silicon MOSFET Technology.

Voltage Ratings and Breakdown Voltage

While there are devices that support higher voltages, silicon MOSFETs are widely used from low-voltage applications through the 600V to 900V classes. Silicon MOSFETs rated at 1,200V and above are available, although their relatively high on-state resistance can limit their suitability for high-current applications. By comparison, IGBTs operate comfortably from 600V to 6,500V.

The blocking voltage range of 500V to 900V represents an application-dependent crossover region where other factors, such as robustness, thermal considerations, and space requirements, guide designers towards the optimal device.

Conduction Losses

Conduction losses are one aspect to be considered during the selection process:

  • MOSFET: Conduction losses are dominated by drain-to-source on-state resistance (RDS(on)). Lower-voltage devices achieve milliohm on-resistance, but this rises sharply with increased voltage rating, penalising applications that handle high continuous currents.
  • IGBT: Conduction losses are dominated by collector-emitter saturation voltage (VCE(sat)). Because the voltage drop increases less dramatically with voltage rating than MOSFET RDS(on), IGBTs often provide lower conduction losses in high-voltage, high-current applications.

Switching losses invert this balance. MOSFET switching losses are dominated by capacitive effects from gate charge and output capacitance, scaling linearly with frequency. IGBT switching losses arise from turn-on diode interaction and turn-off tail currents, which dominate total losses at higher frequencies. At low frequencies, IGBTs yield lower total losses; at high frequencies, the MOSFET's switching-loss advantage is decisive.

Body Diodes and Reverse Recovery

Bridge topologies impose strict demands on diode behaviour:

  • MOSFET body diode: Incorporates an inherent antiparallel diode formed by the device structure. In bridge circuits, reverse-recovery charge and reverse-recovery time cause shoot-through spikes, switching losses, and electromagnetic interference.
  • IGBT: Lacks an inherent body diode, requiring either an external antiparallel freewheeling diode or an integrated co-packed diode whose recovery characteristics dictate switching losses.

Reverse-recovery behaviour directly affects dead-time requirements, switching losses, and electromagnetic interference in half-bridge and full-bridge power converter topologies.

Thermal Performance, Paralleling and Fault Robustness

Operating conditions expose distinct thermal trade-offs:

  • Thermal runaway and paralleling: A MOSFET’s room-temperature resistance can double during operation, helping balance current between paralleled devices and reducing the risk of thermal runaway. Conversely, higher temperatures increase IGBT tail currents, reducing switching efficiency. Paralleling IGBTs generally requires greater attention to VCE(sat) matching and current sharing.
  • Cooling costs: Thermal management depends on electrical losses and operating conditions. Many high-power systems, regardless of the switch selected, require forced-air or liquid cooling.
  • Short-circuit robustness: IGBTs often specify short-circuit withstand times of several microseconds, providing valuable response time for protection circuits. MOSFETs lack such saturation limits, so they require faster protection.
  • Derating: Keeping operating temperatures well below the maximum junction-temperature rating preserves long-term reliability.

Quick Comparison of MOSFET vs. IGBT Device Characteristics

Choosing a MOSFET or IGBT for Your Power Application

Application-Specific Recommendations

While device-level parameters help narrow the choice, final selection depends heavily on the intended application (Table 2).

Silicon MOSFETs dominate low-voltage functions (12V and 48V systems). IGBTs have traditionally been widely used in high-voltage traction inverters, although SiC MOSFETs are increasingly used.

Subsystem voltage and operating frequency dictate the choice, with MOSFETs generally preferred wherever high-frequency performance or lower system voltages are required.

For drive-specific design rules, review the Basics of MOSFETs and IGBTs for Motor Control application analysis.

Emerging Alternatives to MOSFETs and IGBTs

Silicon carbide (SiC) MOSFETs represent a high-voltage, high-frequency alternative that challenges the traditional IGBT domain, offering lower dynamic losses. However, silicon MOSFETs and IGBTs remain the dominant, cost-effective choice for mainstream power conversion today. To evaluate whether next-generation materials change the calculation, review “GaN: Gaining Traction, But Still Short of Fulfilling Its Promise in Power Electronics.”

In summary, low voltage and high switching frequency typically favour MOSFETs, while high voltage, high current, and moderate switching frequencies often favour IGBTs. Selection should always be validated against loss calculations and thermal limits.

item.title: The Ultimate Guide to Silicon MOSFET Technology
item.description:
If there is one silicon device that almost everyone has used, it’s a MOSFET. MOSFET technology underpins applications ranging from integrated digital processors to discrete power switches and analogue amplifiers. This guide focuses primarily on discrete silicon MOSFETs used in power and analogue circuits.

What Does MOSFET Stand For?

A MOSFET is an acronym for a metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor.

MOSFETs are versatile components that come in a variety of sizes, packages, and designs. But which silicon MOSFET is best for a specific application or project? And will silicon MOSFETs remain the most popular choice for years to come?

What Is a Silicon MOSFET?

A silicon MOSFET is a semiconductor device commonly used as an electronic switch or as a power-control element. Its name comes from its structure, which consists of a metal gate separated from a semiconductor channel by a thin insulating oxide layer. Unlike bipolar junction transistors (BJTs), which require continuous base current during conduction, MOSFETs are voltage-controlled devices that can operate as switches or amplifying elements. This insulated-gate structure gives the device a very high input impedance, allowing it to control large currents while requiring very little drive power.

For a quick breakdown of common circuit design queries and troubleshooting tips, refer to MOSFET FAQs.

Silicon MOSFET Structure and Physical Construction

The structural architecture of a discrete silicon MOSFET (Figure 1) dictates its electrical performance, power-handling limits, and suitability for specific applications. A MOSFET is fundamentally a four-terminal device with gate, drain, source, and body terminals. In most discrete power MOSFETs, the body is internally connected to the source, leaving three externally accessible terminals:

  • Gate (G): The control terminal, consisting of a metal or heavily doped polycrystalline silicon layer that is physically and electrically isolated from the substrate.
  • Drain (D): One end of the channel conduction path, conventionally treated as the current-entry terminal for an N-channel MOSFET.
  • Source (S): The terminal used as the reference for gate-to-source voltage and the opposite end of the channel conduction path.

Figure 1: A structural diagram of an N-Channel MOSFET Vs a P-Channel MOSFET. (Source: Mouser)

The defining element of this device structure is the gate insulator, a microscopically thin layer of silicon dioxide (SiO2) grown directly over the silicon substrate. This barrier provides very high DC isolation, requiring almost no steady-state gate current. The discrete power MOSFET structure also creates an intrinsic body diode with a fixed orientation between source and drain. This diode conducts when forward-biased, whereas the enhanced MOSFET channel can conduct current in either direction. The body (or substrate) is the underlying silicon material in which the MOSFET structure is created.

How a Silicon MOSFET Works

MOSFET operation is controlled by the voltage applied between the gate and source terminals (VGS). When the VGS reaches the threshold voltage (VGS(th)), a conductive channel forms. The threshold value represents the onset of conduction at a small specified current, not full enhancement. Switching applications require the gate voltage specified for the desired on-state resistance (RDS(on)) and drain current.

MOSFETs are available in two channel types:

  • N-type (NMOS) devices, which use electrons as the primary charge carriers. Because electrons move more easily through silicon than through holes, NMOS devices typically offer lower RDS(on), higher current capability, and better switching performance. As a result, they are the preferred choice for most power-switching applications.
  • P-type (PMOS) devices use holes as the primary charge carriers. Their lower carrier mobility generally results in higher RDS(on) than comparable NMOS devices. However, PMOS devices remain useful in applications requiring simple high-side switching, where they can be driven directly without specialised gate-drive circuitry.

Silicon MOSFET Types

Silicon MOSFETs are classified by three main criteria: enhancement-mode vs depletion-mode operation, N-channel vs P-channel, and vertical vs. lateral structure.

Enhancement Mode vs. Depletion Mode MOSFETs

The primary distinction between MOSFET operating modes is whether the device is normally on or normally off. Enhancement-mode devices are normally off and require a gate-to-source voltage of the appropriate polarity and magnitude to create a conductive channel. By contrast, depletion-mode devices are normally on. Depletion-mode devices are uncommon, but remain important in specialised applications, such as current sources.

NMOS vs. PMOS: N-Channel and P-Channel MOSFETs

As mentioned, NMOS devices use electrons as their charge carriers, while PMOS devices use holes. Because electrons have higher mobility in silicon, NMOS devices achieve a lower on-resistance and higher current capability. This makes NMOS the preferred choice for most power-switching applications. PMOS devices, however, remain valuable in high-side switching circuits, where they can often be driven more simply than an equivalent NMOS. Therefore, designers frequently use NMOS devices where efficiency is critical and PMOS devices where circuit simplicity is the priority.

Lateral vs.Vertical Structure

While the preceding classifications focused on electrical behaviour, the lateral or vertical structure of a MOSFET describes its physical implementation. This structure affects the voltage rating, current capability, on-resistance, and suitability for specific applications.

Lateral MOSFETs (Figure 2) conduct across the silicon surface, resulting in smaller gate-to-drain and gate-to-source capacitances. However, they typically handle less voltage and current than vertical MOSFETs, making them best suited to integrated circuits, radio frequency (RF) amplifiers, and lower-power applications.

Figure 2: A structural diagram of a lateral silicon MOSFET. (Source: Mouser)

In contrast, vertical MOSFETs (Figure 3) conduct current through the thickness of the silicon die from a top source to a bottom drain. Because lateral layouts are unsuitable for high-voltage applications, nearly all discrete power MOSFETs used in power supplies, motor drives, and inverters employ a vertical structure, allowing much larger current-carrying areas and higher voltage ratings. Modern vertical power MOSFETs are further optimised with trench gate technology, which embeds the gate vertically into the silicon substrate to maximise channel density and minimise RDS(on), and superjunction structures, which use alternating vertical N-type and P-type columns to achieve low resistance while maintaining high breakdown voltage.

Figure 3: A structural diagram of a vertical silicon MOSFET. (Source: Mouser)

For an extensive comparison between these power switches and alternative technologies, consult the guide on whether to use MOSFETs or IGBTs for different power applications.

Silicon MOSFET Design Applications

MOSFETs in Switching Power Supplies

In switched-mode power supplies (SMPS), silicon MOSFETs serve as the primary power switches for converters. Modern high-efficiency converters often use synchronous rectification, replacing passive rectifier diodes with actively controlled MOSFETs to reduce conduction loss associated with diode forward-voltage (VF) drops. Selecting the right device requires balancing RDS(on) and gate charge (Qg) to optimise both conduction and switching losses for the target operating frequency.

Gate Drive Design for Switching MOSFET Applications

During switching, the gate driver must source and sink transient current to move the MOSFET’s gate charge, including the gate-to-drain charge associated with the Miller plateau. Datasheet gate-charge values are generally more useful than the internal capacitance (often represented by Ciss) alone for estimating driver current and switching time requirements. To satisfy these dynamic switching requirements while managing circuit parasitics, voltage offsets, and system safety, gate drive designs rely on several core circuit techniques:

  • Gate resistors (Rg): Tuned to balance switching speed against electromagnetic interference (EMI) ringing caused by circuit parasitics.
  • Galvanic isolation: High-voltage or safety-critical designs use optocouplers, pulse transformers, or digital isolators to protect low-voltage control circuitry.
  • Bootstrap circuits: High-side N-channel MOSFETs require a gate-drive voltage above the switching-node voltage. A bootstrap diode-capacitor network is one common approach, although it requires periodic recharge and may not support continuous 100 percent duty-cycle operation without additional circuitry.

MOSFETs in Motor Control Applications

In motor control systems, silicon MOSFETs are arranged in H-bridge or three-phase inverter networks to drive AC or brushed and brushless DC motors (Figure 4). Achieving high efficiency requires selecting low-RDS(on) devices to minimise conduction losses, along with fast switching edges to minimise transition losses. Designers must provide an appropriate commutation path for inductive current using the bridge devices’ body diodes, actively controlled MOSFET channels, or external freewheeling diodes. Parasitic-inductance voltage overshoot may require additional voltage margin, optimized layout, snubbers, or clamps to keep the MOSFET within its drain-source voltage (VDS) and avalanche limits.

Figure 4: An H-bridge circuit (top) with four MOSFETs, flyback diodes, a DC motor, and an operational truth table. A three-phase BLDC inverter bridge (bottom) featuring six MOSFET switches, PWM control signals, and Wye-connected motor phases U, V, and W.

For details on integrating motor drives, refer to the Basics of MOSFETs and IGBTs for Motor Control application analysis.

MOSFETs as Amplifiers

In amplifier circuits, a MOSFET is operated in its saturation region rather than as an on/off switch. Small changes in the gate-to-source voltage (VGS) produce corresponding changes in drain current, allowing the device to amplify analogue signals. This voltage-controlled behaviour makes MOSFETs widely used in audio amplifiers, RF amplifiers, and analogue signal-processing circuits.

For high-power linear applications, engineers often consider planar MOSFETs because they offer a more robust forward-biased safe operating area than trench devices, which are optimised primarily for switching. Device selection must nevertheless be based on the datasheet safe operating area, pulse duration, junction temperature, and thermal-stability limits.

MOSFETs in Power Management and Load Switching

In power distribution networks, silicon MOSFETs serve as highly efficient electronic switches for load sequencing, reverse-polarity protection, and hot-swap control. Combined with suitable control circuitry, a low-RDS(on) MOSFET can implement an ideal diode function, greatly reducing the voltage drop, power loss, and heat generation associated with conventional diodes.

MOSFETs are also widely used for power-path management. In redundant power supplies, MOSFETs can implement power-supply OR-ing, allowing multiple sources to feed a common rail while blocking reverse current into an inactive or failed source. They are also used for hot-swap and soft-start circuits where controlled gate drive limits inrush current when connecting large capacitive loads. Because the MOSFET may dissipate substantial power in linear operation during startup, its safe operating area must be verified for the expected voltage, current, pulse duration, and temperature.

Silicon MOSFET Selection Guide: Choosing the Right Device

Defining Application Requirements Before Selection

Selecting the right MOSFET begins with understanding the application’s electrical, thermal, mechanical, and environmental requirements. Key electrical parameters include voltage rating, current rating, RDS(on), switching speed, and gate-drive voltage. Thermal considerations determine the cooling strategy and package type, while environmental factors, such as vibration, shock, and operating temperature, may further influence device selection. Once engineers understand these requirements, they can choose a MOSFET technology and package that best suits the intended circuit topology.

Step-by-Step Silicon MOSFET Selection Process

For standard switching applications, MOSFET selection should follow a structured process that considers electrical, thermal, and reliability requirements:

  1. Define topology: Identify the MOSFET’s role (e.g., switch, driver) to set requirements.
  2. Determine voltage rating: Ensure the VDS rating allows sufficient margin for spikes and transients.
  3. Check current and conduction: Select RDS(on) using the root mean square (RMS) and peak currents, the available gate-drive voltage, the temperature-adjusted on-resistance, and the thermal budget.
  4. Confirm gate-drive capability: Verify that the driver provides the required VGS and can source and sink sufficient current to move the specified gate charge (Qg) within the target switching time.
  5. Analyse switching: Evaluate Qg, Miller charge, and capacitances (Coss/Crss) for efficient high-frequency performance.
  6. Evaluate body diode: Check reverse-recovery characteristics (trr/Qrr) for hard-switched or inductive circuits.
  7. Verify fault and transient capability: Check the safe operating area (SOA) for the applicable voltage, current, pulse duration, and temperature. Where avalanche may occur, evaluate the relevant avalanche-current and energy ratings under the datasheet test conditions, including any limits on repetitive operation.
  8. Validate thermal/package: Confirm heat dissipation maintains junction temperature (TJ) within safe limits.
  9. Simulate and test: Validate via Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (SPICE), then bench-test under real-world operating conditions.

How Does a MOSFET Compare to Alternatives?

Wide-bandgap semiconductors, such as gallium nitride (GaN) and silicon carbide (SiC), can operate more efficiently at higher voltages, switching frequencies, and temperatures than conventional silicon devices. These characteristics enable smaller, lighter, and higher-power-density systems. However, silicon MOSFETs benefit from a mature manufacturing ecosystem, lower cost, and widespread availability. As a result, silicon remains the dominant material in the global power semiconductor market, while silicon MOSFETs continue to be widely used in cost-sensitive and mass-market power-conversion applications.[1]

Conclusion

Silicon MOSFETs remain a foundational technology in modern electronic design, offering high input impedance, efficient switching performance, and a mature, cost-effective manufacturing ecosystem. By understanding their operating modes, device structures, and key datasheet parameters, engineers can make informed component selection decisions across applications ranging from power supplies and motor drives to load switching and analogue circuits. Despite the emergence of wide-bandgap technologies such as GaN and SiC, silicon MOSFETs remain the default choice for many power-conversion and control applications due to their availability, reliability, and cost-effectiveness.

To get started with a MOSFET project, explore Mouser’s extensive MOSFET selection.

 

[1] https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/power-semiconductor-market

item.title: IT vs. OT: A Cybersecurity Perspective
item.description:
Source: Alexandr/stock.adobe.com

Information technology (IT) is a complex, interconnected network of business and enterprise systems, such as servers, databases, workstations, and cloud services, that facilitate communication, data exchange, and data storage. Operational technology (OT), on the other hand, controls the physical world through industrial control systems like supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems, distributed control systems (DCSs), and programmable logic controllers (PLCs).

Traditionally, IT and OT have been managed in isolated silos by different teams: IT focused on information flow, and OT focused on process uptime and safety. However, the push for digital transformation throughout industry has merged the two domains to bring operational benefits, including improved efficiency, data-driven insights, and remote control. At the same time, the convergence has exposed critical industrial infrastructure to new cyber threats.

This first installment of our cybersecurity blog series examines the similarities and differences of IT and OT cybersecurity measures, focusing on their impact across industrial automation environments.

Similarities Between IT and OT Cybersecurity

Cybersecurity efforts in IT and OT domains align through a common objective of ensuring operational continuity by protecting systems and data. They apply similar foundational security controls and architectural principles, including defense in depth, asset management, and risk-based decision-making.

The defense-in-depth approach employs multiple layers of security controls, such as network segmentation, access authentication, and incident response plans. The fundamental challenge with IT/OT convergence is not innovating new security principles but adapting and implementing existing ones in a new, physically sensitive environment.

Network Segmentation

Network segmentation techniques contain threats and limit an attack’s lateral movement. In the IT domain, this separation involves differentiating between corporate, guest, and data center networks. In OT, segmentation isolates control networks and critical controllers from general corporate networks.

Access Control

Both domains implement strict access controls and the principle of least privilege. These controls ensure that only authorized personnel and systems have the minimum access required to perform their roles. In OT, there is an inherent need to balance strong security controls with operational requirements to avoid productivity slowdowns.

Incident Response Planning

Incident response plans outline procedures for detecting, containing, and recovering from security incidents. In IT, these plans often focus on data recovery and system restoration. In OT, the priority shifts to safe system recovery and minimizing physical damage and disruption to industrial processes.

IT and OT cybersecurity share the same overarching mission of risk reduction and system protection, and both require a combination of technology and processes to mitigate threats. As OT systems become more intelligent and networked, techniques such as continuous monitoring, anomaly detection, and incident response can be applied to OT just as they are in IT.

Despite these similarities, securing OT is not the same as securing IT. There are critical differences in priorities and constraints.

Differences Between IT and OT Cybersecurity

Although fundamental cybersecurity principles apply to both IT and OT domains, the practical implementation differs due to the system environment and the consequences of an incident. OT systems present unique challenges that make many IT security practices insufficient or require adaptation.

System Environment

OT systems include industrial equipment, such as PLCs, mechanical controllers, sensors, and specialized machines, that run proprietary, vendor-specific software and protocols. Some legacy PLCs are often isolated and self-contained, lacking the built-in security features standard in IT systems, such as host-based firewalls and strong authentication. However, newer industrial devices integrate secure boot, encryption, and role-based access control.

For example, a legacy PLC on an assembly line is unlikely to support host-based security agents or perform resource-intensive encryption. Such devices were never intended to be connected to the internet and therefore lack modern security mechanisms by design.

IT cybersecurity protects general-purpose computing environments with layered defenses, such as firewalls, antivirus software, and endpoint protection. On the other hand, OT cybersecurity must secure highly specialized systems with proprietary architectures that require tailored protective measures rather than direct adoption of IT tools.

Security Priorities

In IT security, most organizations prioritize confidentiality, integrity, and availability (the CIA triad) in that order. Protecting sensitive data from breaches is often the highest priority. If an IT system is hacked, the primary concerns are often data loss, privacy violation, and financial fraud.

In contrast, OT security prioritizes availability and safety. In industrial operations, downtime and loss of control can have severe consequences, and maintaining the continuous operation of equipment is most important. Many OT systems have a direct impact on human and environmental safety. For instance, a cyberattack on a chemical plant or an energy grid could cause physical explosions, toxic releases, and widespread service outages, making this a top priority for any OT approach.

System Life Cycle and Patching Practices

IT and OT domains differ in how they are maintained and updated. Enterprise IT departments regularly apply security patches, software updates, and upgrades. However, OT systems have extremely long life cycles and very infrequent updates. Industrial equipment and control software may be expected to run for a decade or more.

Due to the infrequent and prolonged maintenance windows in OT, many networks operate with unpatched vulnerabilities. These vulnerabilities create rich targets for attackers and complicate the role of security professionals. In OT, security mitigations rely more on compensating controls, such as isolating a vulnerable system, than regular patching. This also implies that incident response in OT may focus on keeping systems running, whereas in IT, it is more acceptable to shut down systems to contain damage.

Conclusion

Though IT and OT are increasingly interconnected, they are not the same—especially regarding cybersecurity. While IT systems include protections for various general-purpose environments, OT systems introduce unique challenges to securing industrial equipment and infrastructure. OT’s risk calculus is fundamentally concerned with physical consequences and safety, changing how organizations prioritize and implement security controls.

In the next part of this blog series, we look further into the challenges of securing OT systems and the complexities arising from IIoT.

item.title: New Tech Tuesdays: Scaling Edge AI Inference with M.2 Modules
item.description:
New Tech Tuesdays

Join Mouser's Technical Content team for a weekly look at all things interesting, new, and noteworthy for design engineers.

Artificial intelligence (AI) processing does not always take place in the cloud. Factory equipment can analyze sensor data on site, while inspection cameras can process images as products move through production. Retail systems are also using local processing for certain AI workloads. In these applications, processing data close to its source reduces the amount of information that must travel over the network and eliminates the need to send data to a remote server before a result is returned.[1]

Moving inference to the edge, however, places a processing burden on the local hardware. The system must provide sufficient computing performance for the AI workload without exceeding the device’s power, space, or thermal constraints. As models grow more complex or a system needs to handle several tasks simultaneously, these constraints become even more significant.

Many edge applications run inference continuously. For example, a camera inspecting a production line might analyze images throughout a production shift. Adding another camera or AI model increases the system’s processing requirements. Increasing the processing workload can also increase power consumption and heat generation. In compact embedded equipment, cooling can be limited, so the hardware must maintain the required inference performance within the system's power and thermal limits.

This week's New Tech Tuesdays examines the role of M.2 AI accelerators in edge computing, highlighting how they can expand neural-network processing performance without requiring a complete redesign of existing embedded platforms.

Adding AI Processing at the Edge

One way to handle a growing inference workload is to use a dedicated AI accelerator alongside the host processor. The accelerator handles neural-network processing, while the host processor continues to run the operating system, application software, and other system functions.

One option for adding dedicated AI processing is an M.2 accelerator module. M.2 is a compact module form factor used for devices ranging from storage and wireless connectivity to other types of expansion hardware. In this case, the accelerator plugs into a compatible M.2 socket and communicates with the host over Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe).[2]

The module must work with the system’s existing hardware and software. Embedded platforms may use x86- or Arm®-based host processors, and developers may create models with frameworks such as TensorFlow or PyTorch, or exchange them using formats such as Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX). Support for common host architectures and model-development ecosystems can simplify integration, although models must still be translated, optimized, and compiled for the accelerator using a comprehensive software toolchain.

The Newest Products for Your Newest Designs®

For systems that require additional inference performance, Hailo-8 M.2 AI Acceleration Modules provide dedicated AI processing via a standard M.2 socket. The modules use the Hailo-8 processor, which delivers up to 26 trillion operations per second (TOPS), and connect to the host via PCIe Gen 3. Hailo offers M.2 Key M, B+M, and A+E versions to support different host configurations.

The modules support both x86- and Arm-based hosts, as well as Linux and Windows operating systems. Models developed with TensorFlow, TensorFlow Lite, Keras, PyTorch, and ONNX are also supported through Hailo's software tools. This enables engineers to add dedicated inference processing while continuing to use the existing host architecture and development tools.

The Hailo-8 also supports simultaneous processing of multiple streams and models. A system that starts with a single inference workload can use the same accelerator to support additional camera streams or models as processing requirements increase. The modules are available with an extended operating temperature range of -40°C to +85°C for embedded and industrial environments.

Tuesday’s Takeaway

Moving AI inference to the edge places greater processing demands on embedded hardware. Dedicated AI accelerators provide an additional way to handle those workloads without placing the entire burden on the host processor. M.2 modules also offer engineers a compact and scalable method for adding AI processing capabilities to existing platforms as inference requirements continue to grow.

[2] https://pcisig.com/specification-overview/pci-express-m2

item.title: Brownfield Machine Data for Plant Modernization
item.description:
Manufacturers can use machine data to improve maintenance and guide further modernization.

Source: Bruno Stock/stock.adobe.com; generated with AI

Connecting existing industrial equipment to new and advanced plant monitoring software gives manufacturers a comprehensive view of different operating data. The challenge then shifts to using this information efficiently to support predictive maintenance and dynamic production schedules.

As more assets are connected, teams need a manageable way to incorporate huge amounts of data into operations and decision-making. Otherwise, simply adding more data will increase the workload of reviewing it without making necessary upgrades to existing operations.

The first part of this brownfield modernization blog series discussed approaches to connecting isolated machines, monitoring motors, and adding vision inspection to production lines. Here, we explore how manufacturers can transform information into maintenance responses, organize mixed-generation equipment around consistent data models, and accurately measure modernization benefits against their full implementation costs.

Transforming Machine Signals into Accountable Maintenance Response

Let’s take an example of a motor monitoring system that reports abnormal vibration. Before maintenance teams can understand the reading, they need to know which motor it belongs to, its operating state, when the measurements were taken, and whether the data is still valid.

This context changes the maintenance team’s response. For example, vibration can rise during the motor start, but an increase that continues during steady operation requires closer inspection. Furthermore, if the measurements are outdated, it cannot establish the motor’s current condition, which can lead to false diagnosis.

An analytics platform organizes these measurements and compares them with established baseline operating rules. Depending on the equipment being monitored, the system can notify maintenance personnel only when a measurement deviation persists for a defined period. But some use cases may require a prompt alert because excessive delay can hide a developing problem.

When an anomaly triggers an alert, its severity should determine the response time. For example, a reliability engineer might review gradual drift during maintenance planning but arrange prompt inspection for a more consequential change. The notification should include the motor identity, recent trend, operating context, and data quality.

If inspection justifies maintenance, a work order in a computerized maintenance management system records the work and responsibility. The inspection findings and subsequent monitored conditions help the maintenance team assess whether the alert was useful and if its settings need adjustment. Ultimately, every actionable alert must lead to a defined response.

Organizing Mixed-Generation Equipment Around Consistent Data Models

Machines from different vendors may define an operating state differently.

For example, “running” could mean that one machine has received a run command and that another is actively producing parts. Engineers therefore need to check these definitions before combining the data. Gateways can translate the communication protocols and make the values accessible, but the state mappings still need to preserve what each machine reports.

For instance, Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC UA) gives measurements, states, and relationships of equipment in a structured information model. On the other hand, Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) distributes published messages through a broker to subscribing applications. These technologies can work together, but neither protocol alone can ensure that applications interpret the information consistently.

Engineers can use a shared asset model to give each machine a persistent identity and organize its measurements, states, and events. They can then map machine-specific information into this structure, aligning names, engineering units, state definitions, timestamps, and data quality information.

From that point, the information can be organized and shared through a unified namespace, giving plant applications a consistent way to find the data they need. For example, an existing inspection result can be made available to production software along with its machine identity, inspection outcome, timestamp, and product context. Production software can then use the defined result without having to interpret the machine’s original data format.

Measuring Retrofit Benefits Against the Full Cost of Modernization

Before retrofitting existing equipment, manufacturers should define the improvements they want and record how the machines currently perform.

If the aim is to shorten unplanned stoppages, engineers can compare downtime duration and troubleshooting time before and after the changes. Other applications may focus on scrap rate, maintenance response time, energy use, or hours spent manually collecting readings.

Comparisons should consider the changes in production volume, product mix, and operating hours. The downtime should be compared with scheduled production hours, or scrap with comparable output, to help separate the retrofit’s effect from changes in demand. Maintenance campaigns and other process changes should also be recorded.

Engineers can directly measure a reduction in troubleshooting time. However, if an alert leads to a repair before a breakdown occurs, the avoided downtime and its cost should be estimated because the failure did not occur.

The value of recovered production also depends on if the plant needs the extra output and could have made it later using spare capacity. The calculation should also use the revenue remaining after variable production costs and count that benefit only once. The cost calculation must also include hardware, integration, installation downtime, software, cybersecurity, calibration, training, and life cycle support.

Measured results can serve as a guide for expansion into assets where the operational need and expected return justify the full cost of modernization.

Conclusion

As manufacturers transform machine signals into accountable actions and organize mixed-generation equipment, brownfield modernization should be guided by evidence from the first deployments. Manufacturers need to know whether the information helped teams make better decisions, whether people acted on it, and whether the improvements justified the cost.

Expansion should therefore focus on machines where demonstrated value supports the next investment and where the organization has the resources to maintain the added capability.

item.title: How Laser Power Beaming Enables In-Flight UAV Charging
item.description:
Source: Sergey/stock.adobe.com

For an uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV), staying in the air longer usually means carrying a larger battery. However, a bigger battery adds weight, which can limit how much equipment the aircraft can carry. Solar power can help, but it depends on weather conditions and the amount of available sunlight. At some point, the aircraft encounters a simple yet challenging constraint: A UAV can carry only a limited amount of onboard energy.

One approach engineers are using to address this challenge is laser power beaming. In this technique, a ground-based laser beam delivers energy to photovoltaic cells on the UAV, allowing it to recharge while remaining in flight. While the concept dates back to the 1960s, several recent tests suggest it is getting closer to practical implementation.[1]

Researchers are working to improve the efficiency of lightweight receivers designed to convert laser energy into electricity aboard UAVs. The US Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) has tested laser power beaming under real-world field conditions. And wireless power technology company PowerLight Technologies has also been working with a fixed-wing UAV, autonomously tracking the aircraft and delivering power to it during flight.[2]

These independent efforts together raise a broader question about UAV endurance. Instead of focusing solely on how much more energy engineers can store onboard, it may be equally important to consider how energy can be delivered to the aircraft while it is operating.

Powering a UAV in Flight

Tom Nugent, co-founder and chief technology officer (CTO) of PowerLight Technologies, describes laser power beaming as a “wireless extension cord” into the sky. The comparison makes the idea sound simple, but building that extension cord requires several technologies to work together. The laser must deliver sufficient energy over distance, the beam must remain aligned with a moving aircraft, and the receiver must convert the incoming light into useful electrical power without adding excess weight or heat.

PowerLight has been testing its Aerial ReCharge™ system with Kraus Hamdani Aerospace’s K1000ULE fixed-wing UAV (Figure 1). During flight, the system tracks the aircraft and directs the laser toward photovoltaic cells tuned to the laser's wavelength. Conventional solar cells are designed to convert a broad spectrum of sunlight, whereas these cells receive a specific wavelength of near-infrared light, allowing them to convert the incoming energy more efficiently. The current system is designed to deliver power at distances of up to 1.6km (1mi).

Figure 1: Kraus Hamdani Aerospace’s K1000ULE fixed-wing UAV equipped with a PowerLight laser power receiver for the Aerial ReCharge™ system. (Source: PowerLight Technologies)

The goal of power beaming is not just to keep the aircraft running while it’s inside the beam. According to Nugent, who also co-authored a book on the theory and practice of power beaming, the system is designed to provide enough power to operate the UAV and its onboard equipment while returning excess energy to the UAV’s battery. The UAV could then leave the beam to carry out a mission, returning when it needs more energy.

The receiver (Figure 2) adds its own weight, but Nugent says its power-to-weight ratio could eventually allow a reduction in battery capacity without sacrificing as much of the UAV’s payload capacity.

“In some cases, we’ve made them so that the power-to-weight ratio is higher than what batteries are, which means that you can do interesting trade-offs as well. For example, let’s get a slightly smaller battery and put on this power beaming, and now we don’t have as much impact on our payload mass budget,” adds Nugent.

Figure 2: PowerLight’s UAV receiver. (Source: PowerLight Technologies)

PowerLight’s current tests involve UAVs that still carry a battery. Nugent says the company’s systems assume that some form of energy storage will remain onboard. If the beam has to shut off, the aircraft still needs enough stored energy to keep flying.

Making Power Beaming Practical

To deliver power to a UAV while it’s in flight, the system must convert electricity into light, convert the light back into energy, manage the heat generated along the way, keep the beam aligned with the moving aircraft, and shut it down safely if something crosses its path. It also has to operate effectively outside a controlled environment (such as a lab).

Efficiency

Efficiency remains a major challenge. Electricity first powers the ground-based laser, which converts electrical energy into light. According to Nugent, today's lasers typically convert energy at 40 to 60 percent efficiency, depending on the type of laser and other factors. When the beam reaches the UAV, the receiver’s photovoltaic cells convert the laser light back into electricity. Nugent says that because the cells can be tuned to the laser's wavelength, the conversion efficiency at the receiver can range from about 40 to 70 percent.

In separate research, the Civil Aviation University of China and Tsinghua University recently approached the receiver side of the problem with a lightweight photovoltaic-thermoelectric design for UAVs. In static tests, the receiver converted 38.49 percent of the incoming laser energy into electricity, enough to power a propeller.[3] The work also addressed heat, a consequence of concentrating laser energy on a small receiver.

Keeping the Beam on Target

Conversion efficiency matters only if the laser energy reaches the receiver in the first place. A UAV is constantly moving, causing vibration and other small disturbances that can shift the receiver relative to the beam.

PowerLight treats this as a cooperative tracking problem. A beacon on the receiver gives the ground system a target to follow, while machine vision, gimbals, and motors on the transmitter adjust the beam as the aircraft moves. The ground-based transmitter system, including the wide-field-of-view camera, beam director, laser power supply, and stabilization hardware, helps track the UAV and direct laser energy toward the airborne receiver (Figure 3). Movement from the aircraft motors and other sources can introduce small amounts of jitter into the tracking system, but the size of the power beam provides some tolerance for such jitter.

Figure 3: PowerLight’s ground-based transmitter includes a wide-field-of-view camera and beam director used as part of the system that tracks the UAV and delivers laser power to the receiver. (Source: PowerLight Technologies)

“Our beam is generally dinner plate size. It's not like the tiny little beam of a laser weapon. So, if we jitter a few centimeters back and forth, that doesn't change the power output very much,” says Nugent.

Outside Factors

To maintain the link, the beam must remain aligned. However, because laser power beaming requires line of sight, weather can affect how much energy reaches the receiver or whether the link works at all. Nugent says rain can reduce the power that reaches the receiver, and heavy fog can block the beam enough to prevent power delivery. The UAV's onboard battery kicks in to keep it flying during those interruptions.

Recent testing by the NRL subjected a laser power-beaming system to much harsher conditions. Working with Boeing and the US Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Ground Vehicle Systems Center, NRL transmitted power across an airfield to remote receivers, with testing continuing despite wind and snow. According to NRL, snowfall eventually approached whiteout conditions and visibility became too poor to continue.[4]

Is It Safe?

Sending a high-power laser through open air raises safety concerns. The near-infrared light that PowerLight uses is invisible, and Nugent says the primary concern is preventing the beam from reaching a person’s eyes. The company uses multiple layers of sensing to detect objects approaching the beam and shut off the laser before they are exposed to it.

PowerLight observed the system’s response during a 2019 test at the Port of Seattle. The team was transmitting power horizontally when the receiver’s telemetry suddenly dropped to zero. The cause was an eagle flying into the beam's path, which triggered the safety system to shut off the laser before the eagle could be exposed.

The system must respond quickly to such external factors. Nugent calls this response the “D³ time”: the time required to detect an object entering the beam, determine whether a shutdown is required, and deactivate the laser. The required response time depends on factors such as the area being monitored and how quickly an object could enter the beam.

Beyond Longer Flight Times

While the most immediate benefit of laser power beaming in this context is extending flight time by delivering power to a UAV in flight, Nugent sees applications that go beyond keeping a single aircraft airborne longer. For example, laser power beaming could enable persistent intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) by allowing a UAV to hover over an area without repeatedly landing to recharge or swap batteries.

PowerLight is also looking further ahead. Nugent says the company is developing designs to reach aircraft operating at 20 km to 30 km above the ground. The aircraft would not necessarily need to remain over a single transmitter. Nugent describes a future network of power-beaming stations that could provide UAVs with multiple battery-recharging locations as they travel.

At higher altitudes, the same approach could also be used for communications. Nugent describes the idea as putting “cell towers in the sky,” with aircraft providing coverage from above rather than relying solely on ground infrastructure.

In addition, PowerLight previously collaborated with Ericsson to demonstrate wireless power delivery to a 5G base station.[5] PowerLight also participated in DARPA's LunA-10 program as part of a Blue Origin-led team to explore power distribution for lunar infrastructure.[6]

For Nugent, the larger opportunity is not only about generating or storing more energy, but also about changing how that energy gets to where it is needed.

Conclusion

Laser power beaming does not eliminate the need for batteries or the engineering constraints associated with keeping a UAV airborne. It introduces challenges related to efficiency, thermal management, tracking, weather, and safety. However, recent work suggests that it is a viable approach for extending UAV endurance. Instead of focusing solely on how much energy an aircraft can carry, engineers can also consider how and where that energy can be delivered during operation.

Like any engineering tool, power beaming presents both advantages and limitations. It may not be suitable for every application, but it provides engineers with an additional option beyond simply increasing battery capacity.
